background.speaker: [target]
background.text: So small business really means local commerce, local communities, and there's probably no other segment that's been more hurt by inflation than our small businesses who have been hit by rising input prices and not able to respond and raise their own prices to customers that much. And so what we've seen is an overwhelming support for the administration's economic agenda, which means that the focus on local business will be supported by more manufacturing domestically, more made domestically. But also making sure that we're reining in government spending that is driving up inflation and crowding out small businesses because of the rising cost of labor, the rising cost of inputs, too much money tracing too few goods. It's basic supply and demand, and that's why I'm so focused on supporting the administration's manufacturing agenda. Most manufacturers are small businesses here, so if we can have more domestic manufacturing, we can alleviate some of that pain for small businesses right here at home.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: You talk about manufacturing, obviously that's been a big focus of the administration for almost a full decade now of his time in national politics. We're taping this on March 3rd. The administration has announced that new tariffs on imports will go into effect tomorrow. Will that increase inflation?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, there's no question we have challenges in our supply chain which have driven inflation to date, in addition to the massive regulatory state during the current administration. So what we have seen during the previous term, when tariffs were implemented, inflation was only 2.1%. And those are tariffs that the current administration largely kept in place. So we know that tariffs are an important tool to advancing domestic interests, as opposed to bringing in foreign-made goods at the cost of domestic manufacturing. So that's a big emphasis as well. And I think what's going to happen in these tariff discussions is we're going to find out that there's not a lot of reciprocal treatment in these conversations. You know, we are charged to take our cars and trucks overseas. And in fact, foreign manufacturers aren't really charged to bring them here. They're charging their cars over here. And we need to level the playing field for all of our businesses, but especially small business.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: Is the thinking behind these tariffs that it may, and I'm speaking perhaps from the administration, from your view, so correct me if I'm wrong, but is the strategy short-term inflationary pain in exchange for long-term stabilizing of these trade relationships?

ground_truth: Well, I don't think that it has bared out that there will be short-term inflationary pain. As I mentioned during the previous administration, inflation was 2.1 percent for the entire four years. And so the focus needs to be on what is the right trade relationship and balance of trade that we should have to have our own economic resilience and stability with domestically-made products. And we've gotten away from that. I came out of business. We know what manufacturing does. It can create economic opportunities. It can create opportunity in communities that haven't had anything for far too long, where domestic industry has been hollowed out in order to send manufacturing overseas. And we have to bring that back.

background.text: Let's talk about a big topic here, and we were actually chatting about it when we came into the room before the cameras started rolling. This has been arguably the marquee legislative effort here under the state capitol. It's the Governor's top priority. He refers to it as tort reform. Opponents call it litigation reform and a number of other names. But at its essence, the proposed litigation reform package, he says, would bring down insurance premiums. He says it would do that by limiting how much certain people in certain cases can recover in civil lawsuits. Now, opponents argue that it won't bring down insurance premiums and that what it will do is bar some people who are legitimately injured from recovering all that they're owed. What's your stance on tort reform?

ground_truth: Well, I applaud the state legislature and the governor's efforts to advance tort reform. I think it's really important for small businesses to have certainty. One of the worst things to operate under in any size business is uncertainty and having unlimited exposures for liabilities. And you can just boil it down to a company operating in the southern part of the city. Someone falls in their parking lot. They may have to close their business. That's a loss to that business owner. It's a loss to the employees. It's a loss to the community. So we have to ensure that we aren't driving our small businesses out of business and shuttering local commerce because of aggressive practices on litigation.
